stories.title: Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes
stories.summary: Warehouses belonging to Russia's second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes. Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes. Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv's "most sensitive economic sectors". Russia has targeted Ukraine's civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals. Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians. Ozon said "a fire broke out" at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday. The company said earlier that a "major fire" was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site. Russia's defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia's children's rights commissioner. Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital. Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated.

stories.title: Japan currently has no plans to supply weapons to Ukraine — Cabinet
stories.summary: Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara noted that Japan had already provided Ukraine with "support in the form of body armor, vehicles, and other equipment from the Ministry of Defense and the Self-Defense Forces"
article_sentences: TOKYO, August 24.
The Japanese government is currently not considering the possibility of supplying weapons to Ukraine as part of its support for Kiev, Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters.

"At this time, the government is not considering the possibility of providing weapons to Ukraine," he said in response to questions about Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky’s earlier remarks to Japan’s Kyodo news agency that Kiev was counting on weapons supplies from Japan, including interceptor missiles for air defense systems.

At the same time, Kihara noted that Japan has already provided Ukraine with "support in the form of body armor, vehicles, and other equipment from the Ministry of Defense and the Self-Defense Forces." The Japanese chief cabinet secretary pledged that Tokyo would continue "to promote public-private support for Ukraine’s reconstruction in close cooperation with the international community in order to strengthen its socioeconomic resilience."
On April 21, the Japanese government officially approved a decision to revise the so-called.
Three Principles on Transfer of Defense Equipment and Technology.
The move effectively lifted restrictions on the export of Japanese weapons, including equipment classified as lethal.

Japan is expected to supply combat weapons only to countries that have signed agreements with Tokyo regarding the conditions for their use, including maintaining secrecy regarding military technologies.

Japan currently has such agreements with 17 countries: the United States, the UK, Australia, India, the Philippines, France, Germany, Malaysia, Italy, Indonesia, Vietnam, Thailand, Sweden, Singapore, the UAE, Mongolia, and Bangladesh.
Decisions on arms exports will be made by Japan’s National Security Council, with the participation of the head of government and several ministers.
Parliament is then expected to be informed of these decisions, but it will not be required to approve such deals.

stories.title: Six million Somalis face acute hunger as drought and conflict worsen
stories.summary: Six million people in Somalia are facing acute hunger, with nearly two million children at emergency levels, as severe drought, conflict and falling humanitarian funding deepen what the UN describes as one of the world’s worst malnutrition crises. Medical charity MSF tells RFI it's sounding the alarm "before it's too late".
